lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you met commas. Where does the comma go in "Kai come here!"? After the name: Kai, come here!
Sometimes a sentence has extra information: interesting, but not needed for the sentence to make sense.

Set it off with a pair of commas: My aunt, a pilot, flies to Tokyo. With brackets: The river (the longest in the country) flooded. With dashes, for a dramatic pause: The cave was silent — then it roared.
The test: take out the extra part. If the sentence still makes sense, the punctuation is right.
Commas are the gentlest, brackets feel like a quiet side note, and dashes grab attention.
Try it in the world: write a sign for your world with extra information set off three ways: commas, brackets and a dash. Take the extra part out: does it still make sense? Next: sentence variety.

exercises.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?
exercises.hint: A pair of commas around the extra part.
choices: My aunt, a pilot, flies to Tokyo.
My aunt a pilot, flies to Tokyo.
My, aunt a pilot flies to Tokyo.
exercises.explain: Commas go on both sides of "a pilot".

exercises.prompt: Brackets can hold extra information.
exercises.hint: Think of "The river (the longest in the country) flooded."
exercises.explain: Yes: brackets set off extra information.

exercises.prompt: Which part is the extra information? "Our dog, Biscuit, loves snow."
exercises.hint: Which part could you take out?
exercises.explain: "Biscuit" is extra: Our dog loves snow.

exercises.prompt: Which marks can set off extra information?
exercises.hint: Look at "My aunt, a pilot, flies to Tokyo." Which marks hold the extra part?
exercises.explain: A pair of commas can.

exercises.prompt: If you take out the extra information, the sentence should still make sense.
exercises.hint: Take "a pilot" out of "My aunt, a pilot, flies to Tokyo". Does it still work?
exercises.explain: Yes: that is the test.

exercises.prompt: Which uses brackets correctly?
exercises.hint: The brackets go round the extra part only.
choices: The Nile (the longest river) flows north.
The Nile (the longest river flows north.)
(The Nile) the longest river flows north.
exercises.explain: Only "the longest river" is inside the brackets.

exercises.prompt: Which uses a dash for a dramatic pause?
exercises.hint: The pause comes before the surprise.
choices: The cave was silent — then it roared.
The cave — was silent then it roared.
exercises.explain: The dash comes just before the surprise.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
exercises.hint: Is there a comma on both sides of the extra part?
exercises.explain: Commas go on both sides of "our teacher".

exercises.prompt: In "My brother, who is ten, plays chess", the extra part is "who is ten".
exercises.hint: Take it out.
exercises.explain: Yes: "My brother plays chess" still makes sense.

exercises.prompt: Which punctuation feels most like a quiet side note?
exercises.hint: Which marks feel like a whisper beside the main sentence?
exercises.explain: Brackets feel like a quiet side note.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is missing its second comma?
exercises.hint: Look for a pair.
choices: Paris, the capital of France is busy.
exercises.explain: It needs: Paris, the capital of France, is busy.

exercises.prompt: Why might a writer choose dashes instead of commas?
exercises.hint: Dashes are dramatic.
exercises.explain: Dashes make the extra part stand out.

exercises.prompt: Take out the words in brackets: "The test (a short one) is today." What is left?
exercises.hint: Remove the brackets and their words.
exercises.explain: "The test is today" still makes sense.

exercises.prompt: "The volcano — still active — rumbled" uses dashes correctly.
exercises.hint: Take out the middle.
exercises.explain: Yes: "The volcano rumbled" still makes sense.

exercises.prompt: Order the marks from gentlest to most attention-grabbing.
exercises.hint: Dashes are the loudest.
exercises.explain: Commas, then brackets, then dashes.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: is the extra part set off correctly?
exercises.hint: Check for a pair: a comma or bracket on each side of the extra part.
exercises.explain: My aunt, a pilot, flies and The Nile (a river) flows north have a pair of marks. Mr Lee our teacher and Our dog, Biscuit are missing one comma each.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence to its marks.
items: It was silent — then it roared.
The test (a short one) is today.
exercises.hint: Look at the marks around the extra part.
exercises.explain: The silent-then-roared sentence uses a dash, the test sentence uses brackets and the Paris sentence uses a pair of commas.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences by the marks around the extra information.
items: It was silent — then it roared.
The test (a short one) is today.
exercises.hint: Look at the marks on each side of the extra part.
exercises.explain: Commas: a pilot, Biscuit. Brackets: a river, a short one. Dashes: then it roared, still active.

exercises.prompt: How many commas are missing? "Mount Everest the highest mountain on Earth is in Asia."
exercises.hint: Find the extra information, then put a mark on each side of it.
exercises.explain: The extra part is 'the highest mountain on Earth', so it needs a comma on each side: 2. Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth, is in Asia.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts in order, with the extra information in the middle.
exercises.hint: Start with who the sentence is about, then the extra part, then what happened.
exercises.explain: Our cat (a sleepy old tabby) slept all day. Take out the brackets and 'Our cat slept all day' still makes sense.
